Latest project finished.

Wooden Mine Truck.

Size:

Length: 15"

Width: 9"

Height: 7 1/2"

Wheel Diameter: 4 1/2"

Wheelbase: 8 3/4"

Features:

Steering: Ackerman Steering

Suspension: Front Beam Axle Suspension

Tray: Lockable tipping action

Materials:

Mainly made from scrap wood. Chassis and tray made from pine, darker wood is mainly merbau decking.

The front beam axle and tyres are made from some mystery hardwood (very hard, very dense).

Various dowels are Tasmanian oak. The only metal part is a short length of 1/4" threaded rod for the

tray tilt lock mechanism.

Construction:

The truck is made to be able to be taken apart (with some difficulty) if anything breaks and needs to be fixed.

For that reason, the chassis is comprised of two main parts that slide together through sliding dovetails at the top and are

fixed in place by tapered sliding dovetails below. The two parts are then held in place with a 3/8" dowel pin that is

hammered into a press fit hole (a 9.5mm hole is a good press fit for 3/8" dowel). The front section is made of laminated alternating

pine and merbau strips to give the look of a radiator on the front of the truck.

Parts laid out before final assembly

https://files.catbox.moe/r8auof.jpg

Splitting the chassis in two allows the parts for the steering and front suspension to be inserted. The steering runs on a simple pin

which is activated by a double pronged dowel thingy. There's enough play to allow for the suspension and steering to work throughout their

range.

Joining the two halves of the chassis

https://files.catbox.moe/bmb12v.jpg

The two diagonal strips of merbau were added near the end. I changed a fair few things during the construction process, which ended up

with a narrow strip of wood in line with the grain taking a large load. Then, when test fitting it I got a bit carried away and hit it

just a bit too hard and snapped the main chassis rail on one side (also cracked the other side as I discoverd later). To add some strength,

I cut a couple of grooves in the sides and glued in some strips of merbau that I had left over from something. It's still probably the weakest

point in the build, and would do it differently if I ever do it again (or revise the design).

Adding in the reinforcements

https://files.catbox.moe/kbc45l.jpg

The headlights were made using some 1/2" dowel and a scrap of merbau. I drilled out the merbau to 1/2" then glued it over the dowel. This was then turned

down to 15mm to fit the holes I drilled with a forstner bit. Once glued in and sanded down they turned out pretty good I think.

Headlights

https://files.catbox.moe/yemmrb.jpg

The tray was made from fairly shitty pallet wood pine, I picked out the least knotted, twisted, cupped and warped bits. The wall thickness is

about 3/8", with roughly 3/16" rabet joints used throughout.

Tray pieces

https://files.catbox.moe/oiaph0.jpg

The tray hinges are rebated into the bottom of the tray for extra strength. I also later added a cross piece for more strength. These were roughly chiselled

out, then cleaned up with my No.71 hand router.

Routing out rebates

https://files.catbox.moe/7vzoim.jpg

The front apron of the tray was strenthened by adding an L shaped strip of merbau along the top of the sides that continued along the apron. This

will hopefully prove strong enough to keep the tray intact for a decent amount of time.

Tray side rails

https://files.catbox.moe/ruc3yy.jpg

I wanted to have a way to lock the tray in whatever position, and also have it look at least a bit like hydraulic rams. So I came up with

a method that uses dowels to create a cam lock on the "cylinders". The lock is comprised of a 1" dowel with a 1/2" dowel running through the middle.

I put the two dowels in a jig and cross drilled 10mm holes offset from the centerline by about 5mm (10mm holes are a sliding fit for 3/8" dowel). The

"cylinders" were made by tapering down some 3/8" dowel in the lathe and gluing it into matching holes crossdrilled into a 1/2" dowel. This made a setup

that looks roughly like twin hydraulic rams when in use.

Tray tilting (locking) mechanism

https://files.catbox.moe/1bakvx.jpg

The Wheels were made by cutting circles out of some random hardwood. I have no idea what it is, but I was pretty sure it had a lot of tannin in it (which I

wanted for the wheels). These were cut a little oversized on the table saw. There was some very minor cupping (maybe 0.5-1.0mm from edge to middle) which I

rectified by chucking up the blanks in my metal lathe and facing them off. Probably not the safest proceedure, but I managed to cut out 12 circles without loosing

any fingers. I then used a quickly made wheel slotting jig to cut the treads. If I make more wheels like these, I'll definitely make a better jig, the spacing of

the cuts is not as even as I would have liked, but you can only see it if you look pretty hard.

Wheel pieces

https://files.catbox.moe/qxqu27.jpg

To keep the two halves reasonably centered during the glue up, I punched 1/4" dowels into the 6mm center holes to stop them sliding in the clamps. The wheels were glued up

in sets of 3. Each group having the slots go the opposite direction. This is important so that the wheels end up being symetrical on the finished truck. The glued up wheels

were sanded round. Then it was back into the lathe. The front wheels had a roughly 1" deep hole cut into the outside. I started with a 40mm forstner bit (that being the largest

bit I had), then used a boring bar to enlarge it to about 3" to be a light press fit for the center hubs. The hubs were made from some light and crappy pallet wood. This was turned round

on the lathe, then bored out with the 40mm forstner bit to leave a deep hole with a flat bottom. The front ones

had some remenant nail holes which I considered scrapping and making more, but decided they looked interesting when plugged with some 3mm merbau dowels that I smashed out on a

home made dowel plate. Other than boring out the hole for the hubs, I chamferred the inside of the hole and both corners of the tread and sanded them smooth.

Drilling holes for the wheel hubs

https://files.catbox.moe/qwpked.jpg

The back wheels were a little different. Here, the inner wheel was much like the front wheel, with a slightly shallower hole bored to accept the wheel hub. The outer wheel was

bored all the way through at 3". The key here was to ensure that the gap between the wheels was consistent and looked right. Initially, I made the gap a bit too small, but I ended

up packing in a thin sliver of wood I had lying around into the bottom of the hole, leaving the final gap at about 5mm.

Boring out an outer wheel.

https://files.catbox.moe/a4nlg5.jpg

Once I had all of the machining done on the tyres, I could make them "black". This was done by ebonising them with Iron Acetate (Iron Acetate is easily made at home by disolving some

iron, in this case steel wool, in white vinegar. Do this in a ventilated area). The strained liquid is brushed on and reacts with the tannins in the wood. Since this wood was very

high in tannins, it turned it all a very nice black.

Ebonising the tyres

https://files.catbox.moe/tn4ojg.jpg

The tyres and hubs could then be glued up and finished with Danish Oil, that brought out the blackness of the tyres even more.

Finished front wheels (before and after oil)

https://files.catbox.moe/n0o896.jpg

Back Wheels

https://files.catbox.moe/54ny06.jpg

The final operation for the wheels was to put them in the lathe and dial in the outer circumference as close as possible. Being wood and me being a rank amature machinist, the runout

is probably somewhere aroung 0.5mm, which should do I think. Then, I could drill the final hole for the axle to go through. This was drilled out at 10mm to allow a sliding fit on the 3/8"

dowel axels.

Drilling the axle holes

https://files.catbox.moe/pjuh1s.jpg

That's really all there is to it. Just a matter of tapping all the pieces together and it was finished. Overall, it's been probably 4 months of work in my spare time. No idea how many hours that

would add up to, but certainly not something that you could ever consider making for a profit. My son is turning two shortly and this will be his birthday present, I think he'll enjoy playing with

it, and I'll get to fix it up when he breaks it.

Couple more photos

https://files.catbox.moe/1rwaxf.jpg

https://files.catbox.moe/e609bc.jpg
